title: Money collected along the way
question: How much do the permitting departments collect in fees, and does it rise and fall with the permits issued and the homes built?
finding: Five departments collected $1.75 billion in permit, plan-check, inspection and licence fees from FY2015 to FY2026 under 72 separately named fees. Building Inspection took in $80.6 million on 71,577 permits in FY2019 ($1,126 a permit) and $95.6 million on 53,662 in FY2026 ($1,781 a permit). Fees to extend an application or permit rose from $218,824 to $890,174 and penalties for work without a permit from $584,745 to $2,488,060; premium plan review, a paid faster service, brought in $5,287,975 at its peak and $414,741 in FY2026. Homes finished went from 3,047 to 1,355.
how: City revenue recorded by the Controller for Building Inspection and Planning (charges for services, licences and fines), and the named permit, plan-check and inspection lines of Fire, Public Works and Public Health, by fiscal year (July to June). Permits are building, electrical and plumbing permits issued in the same fiscal year. Homes are net units completed. Fee lines are named revenue lines bringing in $10,000 or more that year.
limits: Fees are set by ordinance and by law may only recover the cost of the service, so a rise can reflect higher pay and a fee study, not profit; Building Inspection is funded almost wholly by its own fees. Revenue is booked when paid, which can be a different year from the permit. Impact fees and capacity charges are shown apart because they pay for infrastructure, not for processing. FY2026 runs to 30 June 2026.
